name: Sveti Križ Bay Cliff
description: ZAG investigated a coastal rockfall of roughly 2,000 cubic metres between 2019 and 2021, combining geological mapping, geodetic remote sensing and geomechanical laboratory testing of samples taken from the cliff. The University of Ljubljana reports this work as part of the project on erosion of the coastal flysch cliffs with risk assessment.
history: The Strunjan cliff is the highest and the longest flysch sea cliff on the Adriatic, rising to about 80 m at Cape Ronek and running roughly 4 km between Capes Kane and Ronek. It is the longest stretch of undeveloped natural shoreline on the 130 km of coast between Grado in Italy and Savudrija in Croatia. The rock is middle Eocene flysch, a rhythmic alternation of conglomerate, sandstone, mudstone, marlstone and occasional limestone megabeds laid down in deep water about 40 million years ago and later folded and uplifted. Waves cut notches at the base until the overlying sandstone and limestone beds break away, while rain, sun and wind break up the upper face, and the park authority states that the cliff retreats inland at roughly one centimetre a year. Rockfall is frequent and documented: about 2,000 cubic metres of flysch collapsed in late 2019 and blocks of one to six tonnes fell in the bay of Sveti Križ in August 2023. The cliff, its vegetated crest and a 200 m belt of sea below it are protected as a nature reserve inside the Strunjan Landscape Park.

specifications.label: Investigation methods
specifications.value: geological/engineering-geological mapping, UCS and shear lab tests, UAV photogrammetry, LiDAR, GIS hazard/risk maps

source_differences: UL news names researchers from UL NTF Geology, UL FGG and ZAG under project 'Erosion Processes on Coastal Flysch Cliffs with Risk Assessment', it gives no years. The 2019-2021 ZAG years come only from the ZAG annual report, which could not be fetched.
UL article places the 2019 collapse only 'nearby' the 2023 Sv. Križ rockfall, not exactly in the bay.
Years: 2019 to 2021 are not in the ZAG annual report of 2021, which names ZAG as a partner in project J1-2477 without years. The report places the rockfall "v zalivu Sv. Križa v Strunjanu".
